unit.unitOverview:
Name what you are wearing.
Say what the weather is doing.
Say: I am wearing a coat.
Put on a coat when it is cold.
unit.learningPath:
Listen to the lesson.
Words: clothes and weather.
Patterns: I am wearing, and it is raining.
Listen to three short texts.
Say what you are wearing.
Write about a hot day and a cold day.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
functions: Say what you are wearing now
Ask what the weather is like
Say put on and take off
Say a thing is too big or too little

visual.lectureScript:
This is Unit 9. Look at your clothes.
Today you name what you are wearing.
A shirt. Trousers. Shoes. A coat.
Say them with me. Shirt. Trousers. Shoes. Coat.
A hat. A dress.
And the word for all of them: clothes.
Clothes is always more than one.
You never say one clothe.
Now the verb. Wear.
I wear a coat in winter.
And for right now: I am wearing a coat.
Say it with me. I am wearing.
Now the weather. This is why you choose clothes.
It is hot. It is cold.
Say them with me. Hot. Cold.
It is raining. It is windy.
The sun is out. It is a dry day.
And the question. What is the weather like?
It is cold and wet.
Last, two useful pairs.
Put on. Take off.
It is cold, so put on your coat.
It is hot, so take off your coat.
And: this coat is too big.
Too big means bigger than you need.
That is Unit 9. Go and look out of the window.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: I am wearing
grammar.explanation:
Two ways to talk about clothes.
One for every day. One for right now.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Every day:  I wear a coat in winter.
Right now:  I am wearing a coat.

I am wearing
You are wearing
He is wearing
She is wearing
grammar.workedExample:
Somebody asks what you have on.
1. They mean right now.
2. So use am wearing, not wear.
3. Start: I am wearing.
4. Then the thing: a blue shirt.
5. Say: I am wearing a blue shirt.
grammar.commonMistake:
No: I wearing a shirt.
English needs am, is or are before wearing.
Yes: I am wearing a shirt.
grammar.memoryTip: Right now: am wearing. Every day: wear.
grammar.practice:
Write wear or am wearing.
1. Right now I ___ a shirt.
2. In winter I ___ a coat.
3. Today I ___ black shoes.
4. Every day I ___ the same trousers.
grammar.answerKey:
1. am wearing
2. wear
3. am wearing
4. wear
All four? You can talk about now and about every day.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: It is hot. It is raining.
grammar.explanation:
The weather always starts with it.
There is no other word for it.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
It is hot.
It is cold.
It is wet.
It is dry.

It is raining.
The sun is out.
There is a strong wind.

Question: What is the weather like?
grammar.workedExample:
You look out of the window and see rain.
1. Start with it.
2. Then is.
3. Then the weather word: raining.
4. Say: It is raining.
5. Add more: It is raining and it is cold.
grammar.commonMistake:
Do not leave out it.
No: Is hot today.
Yes: It is hot today.
Every language does this differently. English needs it.
grammar.practice:
Make a weather sentence.
1. hot
2. cold
3. wet
4. raining
5. dry
grammar.answerKey:
1. It is hot.
2. It is cold.
3. It is wet.
4. It is raining.
5. It is dry.
All five? Check that every one starts with it.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Put on and take off
grammar.explanation:
Two verbs of two words.
The second word carries the meaning.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Put ON your coat.    (start wearing)
Take OFF your coat.  (stop wearing)

Put on your shoes.
Take off your shoes.

You can also split them:
Put your coat on.
Take your coat off.
grammar.workedExample:
You come inside and it is warm.
1. You want to stop wearing your coat.
2. That is take off.
3. Say: I take off my coat.
4. Or split it: I take my coat off.
5. Both are correct.
grammar.commonMistake:
Do not say: I put my coat.
The word on is not optional.
Yes: I put on my coat.
grammar.memoryTip: On means start. Off means stop.
grammar.practice:
Put on or take off?
1. It is cold outside. ___ your coat.
2. You come inside. ___ your coat.
3. It is raining. ___ a hat.
4. Your shoes are wet. ___ your shoes.
5. It is hot now. ___ your jumper.
6. You go out in the sun. ___ a hat.
grammar.answerKey:
1. Put on
2. Take off
3. Put on
4. Take off
5. Take off
6. Put on
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
grammar.title: Too big, too little
grammar.explanation:
Too is not the same as very.
Very is good. Too is a problem.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The coat is very big.   (it is a big coat)
The coat is too big.    (it does not fit me)

too big / too little
too long / too short
too hot / too cold
grammar.workedExample:
You try a coat and it does not fit.
1. It is bigger than you need.
2. That is a problem, so use too.
3. Say: It is too big.
4. Then ask for help: Have you a smaller one?
5. Do not say very big. That is not a problem.
grammar.commonMistake:
Very big is a description.
Too big is a complaint.
In a shop, the difference matters.
grammar.memoryTip: Too means it is a problem.
grammar.practice:
Very or too?
1. This coat does not fit. It is ___ big.
2. That is a ___ nice dress.
3. I cannot drink this. It is ___ hot.
4. The sun is ___ hot today. I like it.
grammar.answerKey:
1. too
2. very
3. too
4. very
All four? You can complain in a shop now.

teacherNotes.note: Trousers, shoes and clothes have no singular, so a learner will say my trouser is black for a long time. The repair is are, not is, and it is easiest to fix here where all three appear together.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: Too is a complaint, very is a description
teacherNotes.note: This is the pattern a learner needs in a shop and it is not obvious from either word. A learner who says this coat is very big when they mean it does not fit will be handed the same coat again.

teacherNotes.reviewStatus: Script review and curriculum sign-off pending
teacherNotes.noteType: It is raining has no subject in many languages
teacherNotes.note: A learner will drop the it and say is raining. It is not carelessness; their own language does not need a subject there. Say that out loud and the correction stops feeling arbitrary.
